summary: This paper characterizes circuit replication as a supplemental error mitigation strategy by executing QAOA for Maxcut on IBM's 156-qubit Fez platform with up to 6 parallel replicates on graphs with 5–8 nodes. For small graphs, 6 replicates reduce average standard deviation by 108.8% at the cost of 21.8% degradation in inference strength; for larger graphs, inference strength degrades 35.4% while standard deviation decreases only 20.5%, with variability plateauing between 3–4 replicates under the realistic noise model.
motivation: NISQ devices suffer from high error rates and circuit depth constraints; while error correction techniques mitigate noise, they increase depth and resource overhead, motivating investigation of whether simple circuit replication can reduce output variability and serve as a lightweight supplement to more complex error mitigation schemes.
method: Using Qiskit targeting IBM Fez connectivity, QAOA circuits for Maxcut were transpiled with a custom pass that duplicates programs stochastically via the transpiler to induce structural heterogeneity while preserving computational homogeneity, simulated under both noiseless and realistic hardware noise models for replication levels 1–6, and analyzed using inference strength (ratio of successful trial frequency to highest erroneous trial frequency) and standard deviation across ten trials per configuration.
result: Replication stabilizes output variability without improving average inference strength—6 replicates reduce standard deviation by up to 108.8% for small graphs but degrade inference strength by 21.8%–35.4% due to accumulated gate errors, with diminishing returns after 3–4 replicates in noisy simulation, suggesting utility only for large-depth variability-sensitive workloads rather than as a standalone mitigation strategy.
